title: Facilitating Learning — floor exercise
lead: One page. Print it, or open it on a phone. Everything the exercise needs is on it.
quadrantsLead: Tape a circle on the floor and divide it into quarters. Perceiving runs bottom to top: abstract at the bottom, concrete at the top. Processing runs left to right: reflective on the left, active on the right.
promptsLead: In quadrant groups, about 8 minutes each. Take one answer from each quadrant before moving on, so no group hears only itself.
prompts: What does a session feel like when it is run entirely in your quadrant? Name what a participant gets from it, and name what they miss.
Think of a session where you were the one out of step with how it was being run. What did you do — and what could the trainer have done that would have brought you back in?
Which quadrant do you avoid when you plan a session? What would you have to do differently, concretely, to run that part of the cycle properly?
lopsidedLead: Eleven Reflectors and one Activist happens, and the session as written does not handle it. The imbalance is not a problem with the exercise — it is the most interesting thing in the room, provided you say so.
lopsided: **Never leave one person standing alone.** Ask them to join the nearest group and speak as that quadrant's delegate. Standing alone in front of a room is a different exercise from the one you meant to run.

**Say the imbalance out loud and use it.** "This room is nearly all Reflectors. What does that predict about the sessions we design together this week?" That question is worth more than the original three.

**Send the people on a line.** Anyone whose result came out on an edge or at the centre can be placed deliberately into the thin quadrant. Tell them why you are doing it — they are covering a gap, not being corrected.
**If a quadrant is empty, give it to the fullest group.** Ask them to argue that quadrant's case for five minutes. Arguing for the appetite you least share is the actual learning objective.
**Break the big group into pairs.** A group of eleven is not a discussion, it is a queue. Run the three questions in pairs inside the large quadrant, then take one answer from each pair.
**Do not re-run the assessment to get a better spread.** The spread is the data. Rigging it teaches the room that the instrument is a formality.
running: 0–10 min — people arrive with a result. Read out the four quadrant descriptions; ask people to stand.
10–15 min — name the shape of the room. Place the edge and centre results.
15–40 min — the three questions in quadrant groups, one answer taken from each quadrant after each.
40–60 min — whole group: what does a trainer have to do to run all four? Collect concrete moves, not principles.
60–90 min — the rest of the session as planned.
sayThis: This is a preference, not a diagnosis, and the research does not support teaching people according to a measured style. We are standing in quadrants so that you can see the room contains all four, not so that you can be told how you learn.
caution: If someone says the result is wrong about them, they are right and you should say so. The instrument has never been validated. What it can do is start the argument — an argument about what a session misses when a trainer runs only their own quarter of the cycle.
